stem: Harlan’s dissent most directly argues that the Louisiana law

options.text: created racial classes that the Constitution does not allow
was a reasonable use of the state’s police power
options.misconception: Harlan agreed the law was reasonable.

options.text: applied equally to white and Black passengers
options.misconception: Harlan accepted that the law treated both races alike.

options.text: should have been decided by Congress, not the Court
options.misconception: Harlan wanted Congress to decide the case.

rationales.A: Harlan writes that the Constitution “is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.” A law sorting passengers by race builds the very classes the Constitution forbids.
rationales.B: Background: “Reasonable regulation” is Brown’s majority language, not Harlan’s.
rationales.C: Harlan rejects the equal-application claim: the law’s purpose, he writes, was to compel Black passengers to keep to themselves.
rationales.D: Harlan never argues the Court lacks jurisdiction; he argues the Court read the Constitution wrong.
rationales.general:
1. Read Harlan’s rule. The Constitution “is color-blind” and tolerates no classes among citizens.
2. Ask what the law does. It sorts citizens by race into separate cars.
3. Test the other readings. Background: Reasonable regulation is the majority’s phrase; equal application is the claim Harlan rejects.
4. Match the charge. A race-sorting law creates the classes Harlan says the Constitution forbids.
Remember: a dissent states its own rule first — measure the law against that rule.

stimulus.source_note: Plessy v. Ferguson, 163 U.S. 537 (1896). Majority opinion by Justice Henry Billings Brown; dissent by Justice John Marshall Harlan. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
[Majority opinion, Justice Henry Billings Brown:]

“The object of the [Fourteenth] amendment was undoubtedly to enforce the absolute equality of the two races before the law, but, in the nature of things, it could not have been intended to abolish distinctions based upon color, or to enforce social, as distinguished from political, equality. . . . We consider the underlying fallacy of the plaintiff’s argument to consist in the assumption that the enforced separation of the two races stamps the colored race with a badge of inferiority. If this be so, it is not by reason of anything found in the act, but solely because the colored race chooses to put that construction upon it.”

[Dissent, Justice John Marshall Harlan:]

“The thing to accomplish was, under the guise of giving equal accommodation for whites and blacks, to compel the latter to keep to themselves while traveling in railroad passenger coaches. . . . Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.”

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain Supreme Court opinion
